KP22 Robust Statistical Regression and Ridge Regression

Level: undergraduate, year 3

Pattern Recognition | Chapter 4, §4.19.2

Slides: read and download

Learning objectives

  • Explain why least squares fears outliers and write the Huber and ε-insensitive losses.
  • Explain how ε-insensitive regression produces sparsity and the trade-off in ε.
  • Write the closed form and the two forms of ridge regression and compare what each of the four methods resists.

KP22 Robust Statistical Regression and Ridge Regression

One-sentence summary: Least squares is terrified of outliers; with a loss that is lenient on large errors, one bad point no longer bends the line. Huber makes large errors linear, the ε-insensitive loss ignores small errors (and gains sparsity) and ridge regression takes ε=0 to gain a closed form.

1. The outlier

Plain explanation: What does least squares do when one point is badly wrong?

  • Outlier: a point far from the trend of the others (an extreme value or a wrong label); the effect is larger at the edge of the xxx range.

Example (designed here): 20 points y=2x+1+y=2x+1+y=2x+1+ noise (sd 0.3) with x∈[0,4]x\in[0,4]x∈[0,4], plus one outlier at x=5x=5x=5 with yyy raised by 10. The least-squares slope goes 2.009→2.6862.009\to2.6862.009→2.686 and the intercept 1.000→−0.0071.000\to-0.0071.000→−0.007 (truth 2 and 1); three noise draws give 2.69, 2.95 and 2.98. Squaring makes a large error's contribution grow quadratically, so it dominates the solution.

Figure lec05-kp22-outlier: 20 points, the outlier (star) and two least-squares lines.

2. Robust losses

A robust loss is lenient on large errors so that a few bad points no longer dominate. The ε-insensitive loss is max⁡(0,∣e∣−ϵ)\max(0,|e|-\epsilon)max(0,∣e∣−ϵ); errors within ϵ\epsilonϵ cost nothing. The Huber loss:

L={12e2∣e∣≤cc∣e∣−c22∣e∣>c \mathcal L=\begin{cases}\tfrac12e^2 & |e|\le c\\ c|e|-\tfrac{c^2}{2} & |e|>c\end{cases} L={21​e2c∣e∣−2c2​​∣e∣≤c∣e∣>c​

The outlier's influence drops from quadratic to linear. Values: e=3e=3e=3: squared 4.5, Huber (c=1c=1c=1) 2.5, ε-insensitive (ϵ=0.5\epsilon=0.5ϵ=0.5) 2.5; e=10e=10e=10: 50, 9.5, 9.5.

Figure lec05-kp22-losses: three losses against the residual.

3. Huber fit

IRLS (iteratively reweighted least squares): weight 1 when ∣e∣≤c|e|\le c∣e∣≤c and c/∣e∣c/|e|c/∣e∣ otherwise, repeated until convergence. Example (designed here, the same 21 points): Huber (c=1c=1c=1) slope 2.099, intercept 0.867; least squares 2.686, −0.007-0.007−0.007; least squares on clean data 2.009, 1.000. Three noise draws: Huber 2.10, 2.14, 2.13; least squares 2.69, 2.95, 2.98. Huber is still slightly off (truth 2) but far less.

Figure lec05-kp22-hfit: the two lines on the same 21 points.

4. ε-insensitive regression

Formal definition (SVR): minimize 12∥w∥2+C∑(ξi+ξi⋆)\tfrac12\|w\|^2+C\sum(\xi_i+\xi_i^{\star})21​∥w∥2+C∑(ξi​+ξi⋆​) with ∣yi−⟨w,ϕ(xi)⟩−w0∣≤ϵ+|y_i-\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle-w_0|\le\epsilon+∣yi​−⟨w,ϕ(xi​)⟩−w0​∣≤ϵ+ slack; g(x)=∑i(λi⋆−λi)K(x,xi)+w0g(x)=\sum_i(\lambda_i^{\star}-\lambda_i)K(x,x_i)+w_0g(x)=∑i​(λi⋆​−λi​)K(x,xi​)+w0​. Read from KKT: error <ϵ<\epsilon<ϵ → λi=λi⋆=0\lambda_i=\lambda_i^{\star}=0λi​=λi⋆​=0; support vectors = points with error ≥ϵ\ge\epsilon≥ϵ; error >ϵ>\epsilon>ϵ → λ=C\lambda=Cλ=C. ϵ\epsilonϵ is the sparsity knob.

Figure lec05-kp22-svr: the objective, the regressor and the KKT readings.

5. Turning ε

Example (designed here): y=sin⁡x+y=\sin x+y=sinx+ noise (sd 0.15), 60 points, Gaussian kernel γ=0.5\gamma=0.5γ=0.5, C=10C=10C=10. Support vectors: ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01ϵ=0.01: 58; 0.1: 29; 0.2: 9; 0.3: 6; 0.5: 5; 1.0: 2. Mean squared error against the true sin: 0.0008, 0.0020, 0.0038, 0.0175, 0.0551, 0.3455. A larger ϵ\epsilonϵ gives a sparser but coarser fit.

Figure lec05-kp22-eps: support vectors against ϵ\epsilonϵ.

6. Ridge regression

Ridge regression: least squares with a penalty on the norm, done in the RKHS. Set ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0, w0=0w_0=0w0​=0 and use equalities: minimize C∥w∥2+∑ξi2\mathcal C\|w\|^2+\sum\xi_i^2C∥w∥2+∑ξi2​ with C=12C\mathcal C=\tfrac1{2C}C=2C1​. The closed form is g(x)=yT(K+CI)−1pg(x)=y^T(\mathcal K+\mathcal CI)^{-1}pg(x)=yT(K+CI)−1p; it differs from the kernel least squares of KP21 only by CI\mathcal CICI. The price: with ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0 no point is a free zero-error point, so sparsity is lost (the loss became squared and the constraints equalities); there is no free lunch.

Figure lec05-kp22-ridge: the objective, the closed form and the two linear-kernel forms.

7. Collinearity

The two linear-kernel forms: w=(XTX+CI)−1XTy=XT(XXT+CI)−1yw=(X^TX+\mathcal CI)^{-1}X^Ty=X^T(XX^T+\mathcal CI)^{-1}yw=(XTX+CI)−1XTy=XT(XXT+CI)−1y; with 15 points, 4 features and C=0.8\mathcal C=0.8C=0.8 the largest gap is 6×10−166\times10^{-16}6×10−16. Example (designed here): two nearly identical columns (differing by 10−410^{-4}10−4): C=0\mathcal C=0C=0: w=(−170.0,171.0)w=(-170.0,171.0)w=(−170.0,171.0), condition number 5×1085\times10^85×108; C=0.1\mathcal C=0.1C=0.1: (0.49,0.49)(0.49,0.49)(0.49,0.49), condition number 776. Adding a small positive number on the diagonal is a standard numerical stabilizer; the price is coefficients pulled toward 0.

Figure lec05-kp22-collinear: coefficients and condition numbers for different C\mathcal CC.

8. Four methods compared

On the same 21 points with the outlier, slopes (truth 2): least squares 2.686; Huber (c=1c=1c=1) 2.099; ε-insensitive (ϵ=0.5\epsilon=0.5ϵ=0.5, C=10C=10C=10) 2.122; ridge (C=0.1\mathcal C=0.1C=0.1) 2.679. Nonzero coefficients: ε-insensitive has only 4 support vectors; the other three use all 21. To remember: Huber = large errors linear; ε-insensitive = small errors ignored (sparse); ridge = ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0 for a closed form (not sparse). Common misconception: ridge regression resists outliers; in fact it resists collinearity and overfitting, not outliers.

Figure lec05-kp22-compare: slopes and nonzero coefficients of the four methods.

Extension: the threshold c, practice and worked solution

The Huber threshold ccc (the same 21 points): c=0.2c=0.2c=0.2: 2.045; 0.5: 2.054; 1: 2.099; 2: 2.188; 5: 2.455; 20: 2.686. A large ccc puts every error in the quadratic zone, which is least squares; a small ccc nearly ignores the outlier. Choose ccc to match the noise level (sd 0.3 here).

Figure lec05-kp22-csweep: the Huber slope against ccc.
